newsitem.title: THAILAND: SE Asian Grain - Thailand, Malaysia to pick up corn.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian Grain - Thailand, Malaysia to pick up corn.

text.p: Thailand and Malaysia may soon be in the market for at least 250,000 tonnes of corn from either Argentina or China, regional traders said on Wednesday.

Trade sources in Bangkok said the government had approved a zero-tariff corn import quota of 200,000 tonnes for 1997 and feedmillers were poised to begin filing their orders. Thailand wants the corn to arrive before the end of June.

A dealer for a U.S. commodity house in Singapore said that once details of the Thai government's decision were finalised, "the Thais will move faster into the market rather than later. The likely origin will be Argentine corn, and not U.S. corn".
One major Thai feed producer said he was seeking 50,000 tonnes of corn for April/May shipment, most probably from Argentina.
"We will also look at the United States and South Africa. The current prices are a bit expensive, but I guess we need to order soon," he said.
Thailand, a major producer of rice and sugar, approved the 200,000 tonne corn import quota despite a forecast that the corn shortfall in the country could reach 345,000 tonnes.
Traders said Thai conglomerate Charoen Pokphand had earlier booked two 50,000-tonne shipments of optional-origin corn from South America for March and April delivery.

Traders said Thai buyers were unlikely to be interested in Chinese corn. "With the high tariff and surcharge involved, I'm not sure if the industry will be interested in such an option," said a trader from a U.S. dealing house.
Corn prices in Thailand were indicated slightly higher at 4.50 baht a kg from 4.40 baht last week.
Malaysian buyers were also reported making inquiries for between 30,000 and 50,000 tonnes of corn for May/June delivery, Singapore-based dealers said. The likely origin will be China.
Traders in Singapore also reported buying of between 10,000 and 15,000 tonnes of corn from China by a Malaysian group at around US$149-150 C&F a tonne for May shipment.
Importers in Kuala Lumpur could not confirm the figures, although they agreed they were keen to buy at around $142-$143 a tonne C&F.
"We want to wait and see how the market develops," said Johnny Ong, managing director of Ho Seng Chan, one of the main buyers in the Malaysian market.
Ho Seng Chan, which regularly leads block corn purchases with other local importers such as Ql Feedstuff, See Hoy Chan and Lam Guan Chan, said current prices were a bit too high for Malaysian buyers.
"I would consider an attractive price is one between $142 and 143" a tonne, Ong said.
A trader in Singapore, however, said he doubted the price would come down.

"I think the current level will stay," said the trader with an European commodities house in Singapore. "The Chinese were the only ones not really following the Chicago Board's prices, and with them out the market, any discount will be difficult."
The price of bulk corn, ex-factory/godown in Malaysia's central region, was seen unchanged at 400-415 ringgit a tonne, traders said.
Soymeal was at 850 ringgit a tonne for the local material and 845 ringgit a tonne for the imported stuff.
Grade "A" wheat in bags, ex-factory/godown in the central region was at 850 ringgit a tonne while local wheat at 500 ringgit a tonne.
In Indonesia, feedmills were expected to take delivery of some 60,000 tonnes of Chinese corn next month even as imports from the United States continue to arrive, traders said.
They said one feedmill was believed to have bought some 30,000 tonnes of Chinese corn, while a few others were expected to have bought a similar amount.
"The shipments are expected to arrive in April," one trader said. "The price is not quite clear, but China was offering corn at around $150-$152 (a tonne) C&F."
Another trader said there was market talk that shipments from China could total 100,000 tonnes. "I have been hearing that there's plenty of interest in Chinese corn."
"Imports from the United States are continuing to arrive in Jakarta,' he said.
Traders said the harvest in the key growing region of Lampung in South Sumatra was proceeding, but that output had not been as high as last year.
"There seems to be no peak," one said. "I am getting about 150 tonnes per day of the regular and hybrid varieties."
Indonesian corn prices were generally stable at 410-415 rupiah/kg in Jakarta, unchanged from last week.
The traders said soymeal prices were mostly stable at 830 rupiah/kg in Jakarta. They said Indian soymeal was being offered at $330 a tonne C&F, up from $326 a tonne last week.
